column1: # Step 4's view of the version fences it inherits.
# `hold m01.tsv`, `hold m02.tsv` and `hold m03.tsv` bring steps 1 to 3 forward
# as standing rules: a FAIL voids the reading rather than costing a share,
# which is what "the earlier steps must still hold" means here. Six of those
# rules name a Spark version, and every one of them is false at step 4 by
# construction, because step 4's whole first requirement is to move the tree
# off 3.2.4. Left alone they would void every correct step-4 run.
# So they are widened, and the widening is forward only: each rule now admits
# its own version *or* 3.3.4 and nothing below its own floor. That matters,
# because a held rule is a precondition and not a requirement -- it cannot be
# asked to catch a regression it was never about. The regression is caught by
# m04.tsv's `m1-spark-334` and `m1-session-334`, which admit 3.3.4 and nothing
# else. A candidate who moved the pom back to 3.0.3 satisfies the widened
# `held-m1-spark-303` and fails the requirement, which is the correct division:
# the standing rule says "this reading is still a reading of this project", the
# requirement says "and it is at this step's rung".
# This file replaces rules/m03-inherit.tsv in step 4's composition rather than
# stacking on top of it. Both widen the same two m01 ids, and `rules.py`
# replaces an overridden rule in place, so including both would leave the
# winner decided by include order -- readable only by tracing the tree. One
# file states step 4's view of all six, and step03.tsv is untouched.
# The counterexamples are the ones the original rules shipped with, and each
# still breaks its widened rule: 2.4.0 is outside every widened range, and
# 3.0.3 is outside the two 3.2.4-derived ones. `--selftest` is what proves it.
# The `held-` prefix accumulates rather than replaces (rules.py:190-195) and is
# applied before the lookup (rules.py:206-209), so `override:held-<id>` is the
# spelling that reaches a rule a `hold` directive renamed. Writing the bare id
# here would be an error, and writing `held-held-` would be the error the
# step-3 split was made to avoid (NOTES 6.4.2, rules/m03-inherit.tsv).
override:held-m1-spark-303
column5: spark-core for Scala 2.12 resolves at none of 3.0.3, 3.2.4 or 3.3.4; this fence was step 1's pin on 3.0.3 and step 4 widens it to the whole ladder so far, because a tree that has reached this step's own 3.3.4 has satisfied step 1 and must not be read as having abandoned it

column1: override:held-m1-spark-uniform
column5: a Spark artifact resolves to a version that is none of 3.0.3, 3.2.4 or 3.3.4; step 1 asked for 3.0.3 alone and this fence is widened to the rungs the ladder has since passed through, but a fourth Spark version in the graph is still a build that runs whichever one the classpath orders first

column1: override:held-m1-spark-324
column5: the build resolves spark-core_2.12 at neither 3.2.4 nor 3.3.4, so the runtime step 3 targets was never reached; 3.3.4 is accepted here because it is this step's own rung and is past it

column1: override:held-m1-spark-324-uniform
column5: an org.apache.spark artifact resolves at a version that is neither 3.2.4 nor 3.3.4; a build that mixes Spark releases runs whichever one the classpath orders first, and which that is is not a property of the pom

column1: override:held-m1-session-324
column5: no replayed job ran in a Spark 3.2.4 or 3.3.4 session; the pom may say so but the engine the code met did not

column1: override:held-m1-session-uniform
column5: a replayed job ran in a session that was neither Spark 3.2.4 nor 3.3.4, so the run was not uniformly on the runtime this step or the one before it targets
